pitch.short: I spent four years at Harlow & Venn testing whether the profit in a deal was real, on 11 mid-market transactions. Since 2023 I have run deal and finance analysis at Pinewick Paper & Print, where I helped buy a box maker and sell an envelope division.
why_hire: Four years of transaction diligence at Harlow & Venn, eleven deals in the mid-market, rising from analyst to senior before I went in-house at Pinewick Paper & Print in 2023.
On the 2024 Ashgrove Packaging purchase my quality-of-earnings work cut reported EBITDA from ₹46.8 cr to ₹36.4 cr, and the price came down by about ₹78 cr.
Outside working hours I build models of my own: a DCF and practice report on a listed board maker, a family-office LBO and a paper-price tracker that updates itself monthly.
pitch.for_company_template: Why {company}: your mid-market deals are the kind where a careful look at earnings and working capital moves the price, and that is the part of the work I like best.

about.intro: I grew up in Tamsin Bay, studied commerce at Wexcombe College of Commerce and cleared the Harbour Institute's financial reporting papers in one go. In 2019 I joined Harlow & Venn's transaction services team in Larchmont Falls as an analyst and checked the numbers behind mid-market deals in packaging, distribution and printing. I became a senior in 2021. In 2023 I moved in-house to Pinewick Paper & Print, a regional paper and stationery company, where regional manager Gordie Pruitt first described my job as 'the guy who says maybe' and now describes it as 'mission-critical' on a poster.
about.now: Studying for Level 2 of the Northern corporate finance credential, taking guard as a Sunday cricket opener and playing fast chess online most evenings.

qoe-box-maker.context: Pinewick's board, encouraged by Gordie Pruitt and a freshly laminated poster about ambition, wanted to buy Ashgrove Packaging, a family-owned corrugated-box maker in Harrowgate, with the price set at a multiple of FY24 EBITDA. There was no budget for outside advisers, so the buy-side diligence was done in-house by Dennis Hale's accounts team and me. My part as senior analyst was the EBITDA bridge and the net-debt items.
qoe-box-maker.problem: Reported FY24 EBITDA was ₹46.8 cr, up 38% on FY23. Pinewick had to work out how much of that jump would survive once it owned the business.
qoe-box-maker.my_role: Senior Analyst; responsible for the EBITDA bridge and the debt-like items schedule
what_i_did: Converted three years of trial balances from the ledger system to one common account structure, then reconciled each year to the audited statements.
Went through each large item in other income and provisions, and located a ₹3.4 cr release of customer-rebate accruals and a ₹2.7 cr one-off gain on surplus waste paper sitting in EBITDA.
Compared December invoices with the gate dispatch log: ₹1.9 cr had been invoiced before the lorries left the yard.
Built the debt-like items schedule from late pulp-supplier creditors, overdue statutory dues and unfunded gratuity, ₹29 cr in all.
Wrote the findings section, then took Gordie and the board through the EBITDA bridge while Dennis checked the rounding.

decisions.choice: Add back the promoter's cheap rent
decisions.why: The mill land was leased from a promoter family trust at roughly half the market rate. That lease would be renegotiated after the deal, so ₹1.5 cr of the saving was unavailable to a new owner.

decisions.choice: Treat capitalised maintenance labour as an expense
decisions.why: ₹2.1 cr of fitters' wages had been booked as new machinery for the first time in FY24, with no work orders behind it, which flattered the growth.

results.note: headline price cut, per the deal team

qoe-box-maker.learned: The biggest adjustments sat in the December cut-off and the rebate accrual. Both fell in the final month of the year, so I now start any earnings review with that month's journals, while Dennis starts with the rounding.
qoe-box-maker.next: I would also model how adjusted EBITDA feeds the funding plan for a purchase, which the LBO work that followed let me practise.

sell-side-envelope-division.context: In March 2025 the Pinewick board agreed to sell Larch Envelopes, a division with about ₹190 cr of revenue. Gordie Pruitt sponsored the sale and named it Project SOAR on the whiteboard, after which nobody could agree what the letters stood for. I was the analyst on the deal team for the fourteen weeks around the teaser.
sell-side-envelope-division.problem: The team wanted buyers ranked from strategic to financial, benchmarks that careful buyers would accept, and an information memo for whoever signed an NDA.
what_i_did: Screened 54 possible buyers (envelope and packaging companies, office-supplies distributors, funds with print holdings), scoring each on fit, cheque size and deal history.
Assembled trading comps for 14 listed peers plus 28 precedent transactions in paper, packaging and print since 2019.
Wrote the financial overview and track-record chapters of the information memo.
Kept the model aligned with the data room each time Dennis Hale posted new figures, to one decimal place throughout.
Kept a shared tracker of NDAs and buyer questions; Tilly Brandt's data-room sign-in sheet proved the most dependable record of who had really looked.

decisions.choice: Rank financial buyers by portfolio overlap
decisions.why: Funds already holding a stationery distributor or a print business could pay more once synergies were counted, which put them above bigger generalist funds.

decisions.choice: Present EV/EBITDA and EV/Sales comps together
decisions.why: Two peers were barely profitable this year, and EBITDA multiples alone would have stretched the range until it was no use.

results.note: precedent set used in the IM

sell-side-envelope-division.learned: Buyers go straight to the page where two numbers disagree. The hours I spent tying the model to the data room counted for more than any formatting.
sell-side-envelope-division.next: I would like to stay on a process through to signing and the share purchase agreement, which I have so far seen only from the buyer's side.

ferndale-initiation.context: I wrote a complete initiation on Ferndale Board & Tissue, a listed paper maker with board, tissue, labels and a small stationery arm, as a practice in equity research. It went out on my Ledger Lines newsletter, marked as a diploma practice report.
ferndale-initiation.problem: The market prices Ferndale as a steady, unexciting board maker. I wanted to know what has to go right in tissue for the shares to be worth more than that.
what_i_did: Worked through five years of annual reports and results-call transcripts, then forecast revenue and margin by segment out to FY30.
Constructed a DCF with an explicit forecast period and a terminal value, and stress-tested it on WACC and terminal growth.
Compared Ferndale with listed paper and packaging peers on trading multiples.
Drew three tissue margin scenarios and measured how much of the valuation hangs on them.
Sent the draft to two practising analysts from the programme alumni and to Dennis Hale for a rounding check, then reworked the thesis around their comments.

decisions.why: This was a diploma exercise. The report offers a fair-value range with its assumptions and states plainly that it is not investment advice.

decisions.choice: Make tissue margins the central question
decisions.why: In the model each other segment shifted fair value by a few percent, while tissue margins alone shifted it by more than the rest put together.

results.note: newsletter and professional network, first month

ferndale-initiation.learned: The first draft held a thesis and a model that never spoke to each other. Reviewers pushed me to show which assumption drives which slice of value, and the report ended up shorter and clearer.
ferndale-initiation.next: Refresh the model after each set of results and publish a short note on which assumptions moved.

lbo-stationery-distributor.context: In 2025 a Harrowgate family office asked a Brackenridge live project whether it should take a controlling stake in Bellweather Office Supplies, a regional stationery distributor. Two classmates and I had six weeks, and I owned the spreadsheet model.
lbo-stationery-distributor.problem: The family office wanted a return figure for the deal, and a view on the point at which the distributor could no longer service its debt.
what_i_did: Built the five-year LBO in a spreadsheet: how the purchase is funded, how the debt amortises, cash flow and returns.
Drew up three operating cases and pushed each through the same capital structure.
Stepped entry leverage up and down around 3.0x to see where each case ran out of room.
Rechecked the entry-and-exit multiple grid in Python before it reached the slides.
Held assumptions and version notes in a shared wiki, so all three of us edited a single model.

decisions.why: One case would have concealed how quickly the structure strains if school and office orders grow slowly. Three cases gave the client a range around the base.

decisions.choice: Lead with debt capacity, then returns
decisions.why: The client's opening question was about debt. Showing where borrowing stopped working made the return figures more believable.

lbo-stationery-distributor.outcome: The client moved to a term sheet after negotiating a lower entry multiple.
lbo-stationery-distributor.learned: The client reacted to the debt capacity page more than to the IRR. That page now comes first in my models, with the returns derived from it.
lbo-stationery-distributor.next: A quarter-by-quarter covenant test would turn the point where borrowing stops working into a date as well as a figure.

stock-pitch.context: Brackenridge's Investment Club holds a stock-pitch contest, and in 2025 the judges were two fund managers and a retired credit analyst. Two classmates and I formed a team of three, and I led it in pitching Quillmark Stationers, a listed maker of notebooks and envelopes. Marla Finch, Pinewick's top salesperson, entered a rival team and pitched from the sales floor.
stock-pitch.problem: Paper earnings follow mill capacity and pulp prices, so we needed an argument resting on those inputs that the judges could test line by line.
what_i_did: Listed the company's 7 mills with their capacity, so every tonne of volume growth in the model belonged to a named mill.
Derived the pulp-cost view mill by mill, and fed it into the cost line.

Built the bridge from EPS to EPS over three years in Python and a spreadsheet: ₹24 in FY26E rising to ₹35 in FY29E, helped by +6 from volume, +3 from price and +4 from pulp cost, and hurt by −2 from energy (team estimates).
Fitted the whole bridge on a single slide, with each step leading back to the mill list.
Wrote the pitch, delivered it to the judges and fielded their questions.

decisions.why: Capacity and pulp costs vary from mill to mill, and a single company-wide margin would have hidden the source of the earnings change.

decisions.choice: Keep the forecast to three years
decisions.why: Three years could be tied to mill capacity the judges could verify. A longer horizon would have leaned on assumptions that would not survive questioning.

stock-pitch.learned: With the mill list and the pulp line on the slides, the judges could test the bridge one step at a time, so I now put the inputs beside every bridge I build. Marla asked to see the judging sheets, which did not favour her.
stock-pitch.next: After the next set of results, write up where the bridge was right and wrong.

reamsheet.context: The regional pulp traders publish monthly grade prices as PDF tables that are awkward to compare over time. I began Reamsheet on my own in October 2024, during my first term at Brackenridge, after Pinewick's buyers asked whether their contract prices had tracked the market.
reamsheet.problem: To see which grades are getting dearer you need the same grade names every month, but the raw tables reword them from one issue to the next.
what_i_did: Wrote a Python pipeline that fetches each month's price tables, run as a scheduled monthly job.
Standardised the grade names with pandas into 31 paper grades that stay constant from month to month.
Kept the history in DuckDB, which now holds 26 months.
Put a Streamlit app on top that shows which grades are moving and by how much.

decisions.why: A tracker that needs hand-feeding each month soon stops being fed. The scheduled job does it without me.

decisions.choice: Fix the grade names before drawing any chart
decisions.why: Month-on-month comparison only works if all months share the same 31 grades, so cleaning came first.

reamsheet.learned: Grade names ate most of the time; once they were stable, the charts took little effort. The job matched mapping a trial balance at Harlow & Venn.
reamsheet.next: Publish a short monthly note on the largest price moves alongside each refresh.

nwc-peg.context: In 2023 a listed holding group put its stationery-wholesale arm up for sale. Harlow & Venn advised the buyer, and as senior analyst I took the working-capital workstream, working with my manager and two analysts for five weeks.
nwc-peg.problem: The seller put the peg at ₹19 cr, taken from the quietest quarter of the year. A peg drawn from one quarter can miss the school-term swing, and whatever it is set at moves the price paid at completion.
what_i_did: Rebuilt 24 month-ends of working capital from ledger extracts, using pandas.
Corrected the series for the school-term season.
Excluded one-off receivables that would not come back.
Walked the deal team through the month-end series, then the normalised peg, in a dashboard.

decisions.why: Two years of month-ends reveal the seasonal curve, whereas a single quarter gives one point on it.
Receivables that will not recur say nothing about the working capital the business needs day to day, so they were left out of the normal level.

nwc-peg.learned: The peg went through once both sides were looking at the same monthly series. Now I assemble that series before I write down any peg figure.
nwc-peg.next: If I were on the other side of the table I would want the peg worked out before the price is agreed.

cash-forecast.context: Each summer the back-to-school run pushed Pinewick's overdraft towards its limit as the warehouse filled with exercise books. Wendell Odom, the warehouse foreman, calls stock 'a river you cannot argue with'. In 2024 I offered to build a cash forecast.
cash-forecast.problem: Finance could see the order book and the receivables but not the week in which cash would run short ahead of the big dispatches.
cash-forecast.my_role: Own initiative, with Dennis Hale and Wendell Odom
what_i_did: Put together a rolling 13-week cash forecast in a spreadsheet, fed by orders on hand and the age of every receivable.
Arranged for Dennis Hale and me to refresh it each Monday in whole lakh, since he distrusts decimals in a cash forecast.
Imported the receivable ageing with Python so the sheet always received it in one format.
Collected stock-in dates from Wendell, and followed debtor days and peak overdraft use through the next quarter.

decisions.why: Large dispatches are scheduled weeks in advance, so a rolling quarter spans the run-up to each and never goes stale.
Collections were the part of cash Pinewick could influence, and the ageing showed which invoices deserved a chase first.

cash-forecast.learned: What kept the forecast alive was the Monday routine with Dennis. The formulas were the easy bit.
cash-forecast.next: Add a scenario for a late customer payment, the risk finance worries about most.
